name: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn
aliases: persistent pulmonary hypertension of the neonate

reference.source: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care / Avery's Diseases of the Newborn
clinicalPearls: Suspect PPHN in a term or near-term infant with marked hypoxaemia and cyanosis that is out of proportion to the degree of parenchymal lung disease seen on chest imaging
The hallmark is a right-to-left shunt across the patent ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale because pulmonary vascular resistance stays elevated after birth
A pre-ductal to post-ductal oxygen saturation gradient (right hand higher than a lower limb) suggests ductal-level right-to-left shunting
Echocardiography is essential to estimate pulmonary artery pressure, assess shunt direction, evaluate ventricular function, and exclude structural congenital heart disease
Common associations include meconium aspiration, sepsis or pneumonia, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, respiratory distress syndrome, and pulmonary hypoplasia
Management principles centre on optimising oxygenation and lung recruitment, avoiding acidosis and stress, and using inhaled nitric oxide as a selective pulmonary vasodilator
The oxygenation index is used to gauge severity and to guide escalation, with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation reserved for refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn arises from a failure of the normal postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance. In foetal life high pulmonary resistance directs blood away from the lungs through the ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale; at birth lung expansion and rising oxygen normally cause pulmonary vessels to dilate. In PPHN this transition fails because of maladaptation (reactive vasoconstriction from hypoxia, acidosis, or parenchymal disease), maldevelopment (abnormally muscularised pulmonary arteries), or underdevelopment (pulmonary hypoplasia). Sustained high pulmonary resistance maintains right-to-left shunting across the ductus and foramen ovale, producing profound hypoxaemia, and hypoxia and acidosis further raise pulmonary pressure in a self-perpetuating cycle.
additionalDifferentials: Cyanotic congenital heart disease such as transposition of the great arteries or obstructed total anomalous pulmonary venous return
Congenital diaphragmatic hernia with pulmonary hypoplasia
Respiratory distress syndrome or surfactant deficiency
Air leak such as pneumothorax causing acute deterioration
additionalInvestigations: Pre-ductal and post-ductal oxygen saturation and blood gas comparison to demonstrate shunting
Echocardiography to estimate pulmonary pressures, define shunt direction, and exclude structural heart disease
Chest radiograph to characterise parenchymal disease and exclude air leak or diaphragmatic hernia
Serial oxygenation index calculation to grade severity and guide escalation
Sepsis screen including blood culture and inflammatory markers
Continuous monitoring of blood pressure, perfusion, and arterial gases
redFlags: Severe refractory hypoxaemia with a rising oxygenation index despite maximal support
Systemic hypotension and poor perfusion indicating cardiovascular decompensation
Suspected duct-dependent congenital heart disease requiring urgent cardiology input
Deterioration suggesting pneumothorax or other air leak
reference.prognosis: With modern management including inhaled nitric oxide and extracorporeal support most infants survive, but outcome depends heavily on the underlying cause and severity. Prolonged severe hypoxaemia carries a risk of neurodevelopmental impairment and sensorineural hearing loss, so structured follow-up is recommended.
pitfalls: Mistaking PPHN for cyanotic congenital heart disease, or vice versa, without echocardiography
Provoking pulmonary vasoconstriction through excessive handling, pain, hypothermia, or acidosis
Aggressive hyperventilation and over-ventilation causing lung injury without sustained benefit
Failing to recognise and treat coexisting sepsis or an air leak
Delaying referral for extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in deteriorating refractory disease
references: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care
management: Optimise oxygenation and lung recruitment with gentle ventilation and surfactant for parenchymal disease, avoiding hyperoxia and lung overdistension
Inhaled nitric oxide as the selective pulmonary vasodilator of choice
Maintain adequate systemic blood pressure with fluids and inotropic or vasopressor support and correct metabolic acidosis to reduce right-to-left shunting
Provide sedation, analgesia and minimal handling to avoid agitation-triggered deterioration, and prevent hypothermia
Treat the underlying cause such as sepsis, pneumonia, meconium aspiration, respiratory distress syndrome or pulmonary hypoplasia
Escalate to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for refractory hypoxaemia with a persistently rising oxygenation index
Use echocardiography to guide vasodilator and haemodynamic therapy and to exclude structural congenital heart disease
Institute structured neurodevelopmental and audiological follow-up
